newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Debt still way of life in unruly Russian economy.
newsitem.headline: Debt still way of life in unruly Russian economy.

text.p: It is easy to spread the blame for a cash crisis snaking through Russia's ill-regulated economy, where workers take to the streets because they have not been paid for months.
The government, admitting it owes money to teachers, soldiers and public sector workers, says companies are hiding money from the taxman.
Firms blame customers, including the government, who do not pay their bills. Workers ask simply for money they are owed.

"The crisis in public financing is Russia's next big problem," said Christopher Granville, economist at United City Bank. "Some really hard lessons are going to have to be learned by all concerned, just as they were with stabilisation."
The non-payments affect both tax bills and wages in the public and private sectors.

Wage arrears totalled almost 43 trillion roubles ($7.90 billion) this month -- up from 30 trillion in June -- and tax revenues are well behind schedule, a factor worrying a delegation of experts from the International Monetary Fund looking at the Russian economy.
"Wage non-payment is the main problem which can blow up the situation in the country," a senior trade union official told the lower house of parliament this week,
"Then there will be none of the (economic) stabilisation we are talking about."
He said wage arrears averaged five or six months and some workers had not been paid for more than a year.
Government efforts to crack down on the situation centre on the creation of a special tax commission which has already promised tough measures against companies which do not pay their bills.
The VChK tax commission shares the initials of the feared Soviet-era secret police of Felix Dzerzhinsky and many Russians expect it to clamp down on tax evaders in a draconian way.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Tuesday the government would start bankruptcy proceedings against four companies that owe large sums to the federal budget.
Presidential chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais promised punitive measures and said this could include making company bosses personally responsible for unpaid bills.
But economists find it hard to identify the first link in the chain of non-payments. There are few efficient mechanisms to collect tax and few sanctions against those who fail to pay.
"What they have to do is start closing down non-viable firms," said Renaissance Capital chief economist Roland Nash.
"If the government keeps coming down hard on firms which have not paid up, I think a lot of them will suddenly find the money to pay, but it is not going to happen overnight."
The focus on the problem of non-payments has overshadowed relatively good news on the Russian economy.
Monthly inflation is expected to be just over one percent this month, well above September's 0.2 percent but down from 20 percent rates at the start of last year.
Officials say the budget deficit has been kept low but economists say this is largely because the government has decided not to pay its bills.

"Non-payment is probably the lesser of two evils," said Nash. "The alternative would be to borrow more on the GKO (treasury bill) market, and that would endanger the whole stabilisation process." ($1=5446 Rouble)
